perspective:
I am Gloria Bangura, an administrative assistant at a large event-planning company. I know Donald Ortega as a bartender who works company events; we are colleagues but not personally close.

Over several company events, I observed Donald serving drinks with little enthusiasm and acting distracted. I thought he might be unhappy with his job.

At a busy company event, I asked Donald if we could talk and told him he had seemed off lately. I asked if everything was okay with the job. Donald told me he guessed he wasn’t as into it as before and that it felt repetitive.

Later, I told Donald I had been thinking about our last talk. I suggested that when work feels overwhelming, something else might be bothering him, and I asked if he had considered talking to a professional. Donald said he hadn’t really considered that and wasn’t sure it would help.

After that, I sensed a change in Donald’s behavior toward me and worried he might resent me or think I had overstepped. I told him I hoped he hadn’t taken my suggestion the wrong way, that I cared, and that I hadn’t meant to overstep or make assumptions. Donald said it was okay, he had been taken aback at first, but he knew I meant well, and it was a lot to process.

I felt the apology was well received and the tension eased. I wanted to strengthen our professional relationship. I knew about an upcoming project and invited Donald to collaborate, saying his creative input could help. Donald thanked me, said he appreciated it, wanted to be more involved, and thought it sounded like a great opportunity.

After we collaborated successfully, I observed Donald making significant contributions and showing renewed enthusiasm. I believed he was valuable to the team and decided to make sure he felt appreciated. During a meeting, I publicly acknowledged his incredible work, said his efforts were crucial, and said his contributions should be recognized. Donald thanked me, said it meant a lot, was glad to contribute, and felt great to be appreciated.
